documents.abstract: This study examines the adoption, use, and institutionalisation of big data and artificial intelligence in official statistics in Latin America and the Caribbean, drawing on the 2024 and 2025 International Consultations conducted with National Statistical Offices. The study combines questionnaire data from 15 responding countries in 2024 and 21 countries and territories in 2025 with qualitative evidence from in-depth interviews. It also proposes the Statistical Innovation Index, a composite indicator designed to approximate differences in the adoption, integration, and institutionalisation of big data and AI across NSOs. Results indicate a gradual consolidation of big data use, although applications remain concentrated in web scraping and satellite imagery, particularly for price, population, environmental, and agricultural statistics. AI adoption remains at an earlier stage: 39% of responding NSOs reported its use, mainly in data processing and other operational tasks. The maturity classification reveals substantial heterogeneity across the region, with most NSOs concentrated in early or emerging stages of statistical innovation. Findings suggest that progress follows a selective process in which exploratory initiatives are gradually filtered into a smaller number of sustainable applications. Institutional capacity, governance, infrastructure, and regional cooperation emerge as key enablers of this process. More broadly, the findings suggest that the transition from exploratory to operational uses of big data and AI reflects an evolving institutional role of NSOs, in which technological innovation is accompanied by new responsibilities for data governance, institutional coordination, and maintaining public trust in official statistics.

Universities increasingly orchestrate teaching and learning through compound configurations that span spaces, devices, timetables and roles. As digital content and workflows increasingly shape physical estates, and vice versa, alignment frames overlook the compound, cross-host configurations already in motion. In this article we ask whether estate-level orchestration, rather than digital–physical alignment alone, should be the operative unit of design for planning and delivering student experiences across and beyond campus. We draw on three exemplars at a research-intensive university: (1) a theatre-scale interactive three-dimensional system, which streams or web-delivers interactive three-dimension into traditional lecture theatres and learners’ devices; (2) a high-fidelity virtual reality digital twin of a chemistry lab for pre-lab rehearsal; and (3) space-planning web apps for co-design and decision support. From these, we sketch a purpose-orientated, configuration-first stance and situate it within work on cyber-/smart-campus estates, learning ecologies, TPACK and postdigital perspectives. Beyond education, digital-first space planning is already operational at scale, including in automotive manufacturing (BMW Group), cultural architecture (Dubai Museum of the Future) and national infrastructure (National Grid’s Triton platform). Higher education has both the conceptual case and, in several respects, the enabling conditions to follow. Hence, we argue that the convergence of immersive, computational and spatial technologies is expanding what institutions can compose and deliver, making device-label categories less useful for both learning and space design. This configuration-first stance is also directly applicable to the governance of artificial intelligence in higher education: as with earlier technology labels, institutions risk misallocating attention and resource if ‘artificial intelligence’ is treated as a discrete category rather than as a family of capabilities, from generative code or audiovisual models to computer vision and wearable ‘artificial intelligence’, some of which already permeate the configurations described here. We conclude with operational implications and a call for institutions to transcend their siloed functions and budgets, by elevating orchestration (not devices, spaces or platforms) as the primary unit of design.

Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence. We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence. We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an $85\times$ reduction in data.

La expansión de la inteligencia artificial en la comunidad educativa y profesional está transformando la creación de contenidos, generando oportunidades y desafíos que requieren análisis contextualizados. Este estudio examina los niveles de conocimiento, frecuencia de uso y ventajas percibidas de la IA en usuarios de Ecuador y Perú, países con sistemas educativos comparables. Se aplicó una metodología cuantitativa mediante encuesta a 493 participantes, entre estudiantes universitarios y profesionales. Los resultados evidencian una relación positiva entre conocimiento y uso frecuente de IA, con diferencias por región, edad y género. Destaca el uso de herramientas generativas como ChatGPT y el crecimiento de Canva IA en creación visual, confirmando el impacto transformador de la IA en la comunicación académica y profesional.

documents.abstract: Peracetic acid-based advanced oxidation processes (PAA-AOPs) have garnered significant interest in water treatment due to the high efficiency, low toxicity, and minimal pH dependence. However, single transition metal catalytic systems often suffer from limited pH adaptability, surface passivation, metal leaching, and a narrow spectrum of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. To overcome these bottlenecks, transition metal-mediated composite PAA-AOPs have been developed, which integrated synergistic components such as secondary metals, sulfur modifiers, reductants, chelators, or external energy inputs. This review systematically summarized the current development of these composite systems, with a focus on the construction strategies and underlying mechanisms for enhanced PAA activation. The synergistic effects driving bimetallic redox cycles, electron donation, metal-ligand complexation, and energy-assisted electron transfer were critically examined, alongside the generation pathways of both radical and non-radical ROS. Furthermore, the key factors governing process performance, like solution pH, catalyst and PAA dosages, reductant/chelator concentrations, and water matrix constituents were evaluated. The practical application potential of these systems was assessed in terms of catalyst stability, performance in real water matrices, and ecological toxicity reduction. Finally, this review offered prospects for future research, emphasizing the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning to accelerate catalyst design and process optimization, advancing the development of intelligent, efficient, and low-carbon water treatment technologies.

Artificial-intelligence-enabled cloud services are becoming increasingly important for digital transformation, but users may not adopt these services simply because they believe the technology is useful. This study examines the factors associated with adoption intention toward AI-enabled IBM Cloud services in Bangladesh, with particular attention to performance expectations, trust, technology readiness and digital skills readiness. The analysis uses the Group 5 survey database, which contains 400 records. After applying the prespecified attention-check criterion, 385 cases were retained for the main analysis. The database contains 30 five-point Likert-scale items representing 10 constructs: perceived usefulness, relative advantage, compatibility, innovation adoption readiness, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, trust, technology readiness, digital skills readiness and adoption intention. Descriptive statistics, reliability and measurement diagnostics, hierarchical regression, bootstrap analysis and importance-performance analysis were used to examine the data. Overall adoption intention was positive (M=3.79, SD=0.48). The full regression model explained 30.5% of the variance in adoption intention. Technology readiness was the strongest unique predictor (β=.224, p<.001), followed by performance expectancy (β=.157, p=.001), digital skills readiness (β=.147, p=.002) and trust (β=.140, p=.003). Adding the trust and readiness variables increased the explained variance by 11.6 percentage points (ΔR²=.116), showing that these factors provide important information beyond innovation attributes and UTAUT-oriented expectations. An exploratory indirect pathway was also observed: technology readiness was positively related to digital skills readiness, which was in turn related to adoption intention. The bootstrapped indirect effect was positive (ab=.067, 95% CI [.031, .108]). These findings suggest that AI-enabled cloud adoption is not only a question of perceived technological value; it also depends on whether users feel prepared, digitally capable and sufficiently confident in the cloud provider. However, all ten three-item scales showed Cronbach's alpha values below .70, and several discriminant-validity indicators were elevated. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted as data-grounded associations rather than as definitive confirmation of a latent-variable model. The main contribution of the study is a readiness-centered interpretation of AI-enabled cloud adoption in the Bangladesh context, together with a clear recommendation for future scale validation and confirmatory testing.

This study examined the perceptions of pre-service teachers regarding the Spanish government’s response to the misuse of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) for creating disinformation, as well as the mitigation of risks associated with deepfakes produced using these digital tools. A quantitative methodology was employed, involving 133 pre-service teachers pursuing a Primary Education degree in the Region of Murcia (Spain) who participated voluntarily. The results revealed low levels of confidence in the government’s response to these online threats. However, a minority of participants expressed greater confidence in the government and focused more on the risk of generative AI being misused to amplify manipulative disinformation campaigns. Raising awareness about the link between pre-service teachers’ knowledge of this issue and the government’s response could prompt educational authorities to take action and establish boundaries regarding the weaponisation potential of deepfakes. Specifically, further research within higher education programs is needed to help students master digital citizenship competencies that enable them to identify tactics of digital political manipulation, evaluate the motivations underlying the sources, and adopt preventive tracking mechanisms to rebuild the trust in authentic political information digitally accessible.

Purpose This study aims to investigate the impact of protean and boundaryless career orientations on organizational commitment among fractional executives. This group represents a growing workforce segment that provides part-time and project-based executive services across multiple organizations simultaneously. Fractional executives are more likely to embody unique attitudes toward career progression and organizational loyalty. Design/methodology/approach The authors collected survey data from 169 fractional executives across diverse industries to examine how these career orientations influence affective, normative and continuance commitment. Necessary condition analysis (NCA) was used for data analysis. Findings The NCA analysis showed that protean attitudes, characterized by self-direction and values-driven motivation, were significant predictors of overall organizational commitment and, more specifically, of affective commitment. However, these attitudes were not necessary for continuance or normative commitment. Boundaryless career attitudes produced mixed results. Mobility preference predicted affective commitment, whereas psychological flexibility showed no significant relationship with continuance or normative commitment. Originality/value These findings advance understanding of leadership commitment in flexible work structures and offer practical insight for organizations engaging high-level fractional executives. The results stress the importance of aligning work design and leadership expectations with the career values of protean and boundaryless oriented professionals. They also provide practical guidance for organizations seeking to design fractional leadership arrangements that enhance commitment and performance. The study concludes with practical implications, limitations and avenues for future research.

AI-assisted tooling is increasingly being integrated into infrastructure management, security operations, software engineering, and scientific computing environments. While discussion around AI adoption often emphasizes automation and productivity, expert users still need to understand what these systems are doing, decide when to trust their recommendations, and know what to do when the system is wrong or uncertain. This talk synthesizes findings and observations from UX research across enterprise data classification, identity and access management (IAM), backup and recovery, ransomware resilience, and AI-assisted infrastructure workflows. The evidence includes studies with cloud developers, security and compliance practitioners, and IT and site reliability professionals, alongside ongoing design and research work examining how expert users interact with AI-supported technical systems. Across these domains, three recurring usability challenges emerge: unclear system state, difficulty evaluating AI-generated recommendations, and limited support for correcting or recovering from AI-supported actions when something goes wrong. Although the technical environments differ, users repeatedly need to understand what the system observed or changed, evaluate whether a recommendation is appropriate for their specific context, and determine what to verify, reverse, or escalate before taking consequential action. These challenges have direct implications for research software engineering. AI-assisted code generation, workflow scripting, cloud and HPC configuration, notebook assistants, debugging, testing, and scientific automation introduce similar questions about visibility, trust, accountability, and recoverability. Lessons from enterprise infrastructure and security therefore provide useful design considerations for RSEs evaluating or building AI-assisted research software. The session offers a cross-domain synthesis of these recurring human-AI interaction challenges and practical questions for evaluating AI-assisted systems. Attendees will leave with a set of questions they can use to evaluate AI-assisted systems: whether users can understand system state, decide when to rely on a recommendation and when to question it, intervene when necessary, and verify or recover from the resulting actions. Connection to Mission, Goals, & Interests of US-RSE Community This talk aligns closely with the USRSE’26 theme, “Advancing Science in the Age of AI,” by focusing on the human and operational challenges that emerge as AI-assisted tooling is integrated into technical and scientific workflows. My background is in UX research and human factors across enterprise infrastructure, cloud systems, security tooling, and scientific software environments. Across these domains, I have observed the same challenges emerge when expert users interact with AI systems, including issues with transparency, trust calibration, oversight, error recovery, and workflow integration. While conversations around AI often emphasize capability and productivity, this session examines how usability and human-centered design influence the successful adoption of AI within complex environments. These topics are directly relevant to research software engineers who develop, evaluate, maintain, or adopt AI-assisted tools as part of scientific workflows. The goal of this session is to encourage discussion around designing AI systems that better support expert users while maintaining reliability, transparency, and human understanding. These topics connect strongly with the US-RSE community’s broader interests in sustainable, usable, and effective research software.

Background Effective communication is fundamental to high-quality healthcare. Communication skills training is a core component of medical curricula, yet opportunities to practice with standardized patients (SPs) are limited, costly, and can elicit anxiety in novice learners. Generative AI (GenAI) virtual patients may offer a scalable and accessible supplement. This quasi-experimental study examined the effect of practicing with a GenAI-patient on medical students’ self-reported nervousness, preparedness, self-efficacy, and self-perceived competence during their first SP encounter. Materials and methods First-year medical students ( n = 383) at the University of Amsterdam were allocated on the basis of the class schedule to a control group receiving standard e-learning preparation ( n = 182) or an intervention group offered voluntary additional access to a GenAI-patient built on a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework using GPT-4o ( n = 201). Students completed a 31-item questionnaire after their first SP class. Primary outcomes were nervousness, preparedness, self-efficacy, and self-perceived competence. Group differences were assessed using Mann–Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The primary analysis was by intention-to-treat, comparing all students allocated to the intervention with all control students; the comparison restricted to actual users of the tool was secondary. Results Of 180 students that completed the questionnaire, 84 were controls and 96 students were allocated to the intervention, of whom 49 had used the GenAI-patient. No statistically significant differences were found between groups on the outcomes after FDR correction. In the intention-to-treat analysis; all composite effect sizes were near zero (Cliff's delta −0.05 to 0.04, all 95% confidence intervals including zero), as were those in the per-protocol comparison (−0.12 to 0.07). Among tool users, experience was generally positive: 63%–71% gave positive ratings. The majority considered the GenAI-patient a valuable contribution to the standard class preparation (71%). Conclusions Voluntary, single-session text-based practice with a GenAI-patient did not significantly reduce nervousness or improve self-assessed communication competence before a first SP encounter. Positive user experience suggests potential for the format, provided future iterations incorporate mandatory minimum engagement, multiple patient cases, automated feedback, and higher-fidelity multimodal interaction.

documents.abstract: This lecture for MSc students in aerospace engineering presents a workflow for research with AI agents, from the author's evaluation of large language models between ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 3, Gemini 3.1, and Claude Opus 5.5. A use case shows an agent building a verified and validated Abaqus model of the double cantilever beam benchmarks of Krueger (2008) in one morning, with the researcher answering the decisive questions at checkpoints. The lecture discusses the responsible use of AI, how AI changes highly technical work, the growing role of experiments, and what this means for junior engineers. Lecture Given on 19 October 2026 as part of the Aerospace Structures and Materials core, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Delft University of Technology, Delft, The Netherlands. Contents Motivation for this lecture: why, after evaluating the new large language models every summer, Claude Opus 5 (August 2026) changed the author's way of working, and why the lecture was given now. Learning objectives: understand, evaluate and apply the author's way of working with novel AI models; create your own way of working with them; re-evaluate the role of a junior engineer in a world with AI. A brief history of large language models: from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-4 (2023). How AI entered my research/education workflows: ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 3, Gemini 3.1, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 5.5, and an analogy of three kinds of helpers. What fits inside current LLMs: tokens, context windows measured in papers, parameters against context, and the context of one agent session. Responsible use of AI: three rules, with a discussion: "Everything that can be automated should be automated"; "Focus on the crucial things, avoid the trivial things"; "Never delegate the decisions that make your work yours". My workflow with AI: a working folder in an integrated development environment, Claude as the agent, an HPC cluster as the simulation environment, and the state of the work kept in files (README, DECISIONS, REPORT), not in the chat. Consequences of a workflow with AI: how research moves forward through verification, validation and new hypotheses; where AI can take over parts of this process; what changed in the author's work. Use case: a verified DCB model: the prompt (goal, ten ground rules, phases with checkpoints), one morning by the clock, and where the model stood at the end of it. Figures as code: TikZ: vector figures written by the agent from the models' own data. How has AI changed highly technical jobs: numerical work and theoretical research; the shift from executing calculations to synthesis and verification; why experiments matter more, including AI combined with mechanical testing. The AI workflow of a junior engineer: how engineers grew until about 2024, judging what the AI produces, and two discussions. Take-home messages. The use case The agent built an Abaqus model of the double cantilever beam (DCB) benchmarks of the NASA report by Krueger (2008), NASA/TM-2008-215123, following a prompt written as a contract: every value with its source, every analysis through scripts, failed runs kept, and stops at two checkpoints where the researcher decides. In one morning, the agent completed the environment check and the reference card (09:46 to 10:07), wrote the plan after the researcher's decisions at the first checkpoint (11:23 to 11:29), and built and verified the model after the second checkpoint: the first models ran at 12:07, and the model worked at 13:23. At that point, the unidirectional model agreed with the published Marc 3D results of Orifici and Krueger (2010) within 0.1 to 0.6 %, and with the 2008 report within 0.1 to 0.8 % once its crack fronts were taken 0.5 mm beyond the labelled lengths; the acceptance criterion of the approved plan was 2 %. Running the use case The file use-case.zip contains the prompt of the use case, PROMPT_use_case.md. The report it works from is not included; to run the use case: Download the report by Krueger (2008), NASA/TM-2008-215123, from the NASA Technical Reports Server, where it is available free of charge: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20080015439. In your project folder, create a subfolder named references and save the report there as references/krueger2008NASA.pdf. The file name is the key of the case: if the agent does not find this file, it stops and asks. Place the prompt in the project folder, and check that its cluster settings suit your environment: ground rule 4 submits every analysis with qsub, and Phase 0 loads Abaqus in the cluster. Open the project folder with an AI coding agent (in the lecture: Claude, in an integrated development environment), and ask it to read the prompt and start with Phase 0. The agent creates the case folder krueger2008NASA_dcb next to references, and stops at two checkpoints for your decisions. Requirements: Abaqus with a valid licence, including its Python for scripting and post-processing; a computer or cluster to run the analyses; and Python for the work outside Abaqus, such as digitising figures. Take-home messages Write the prompt as a contract: definitions, ground rules, phases, and checkpoints where the agent stops and asks. Keep the state in files (README, DECISIONS, REPORT), not in the chat: someone else can reproduce every number. Automate everything that can be automated, and keep the focus on the crucial things. Let the agent verify and look for evidence; you judge the evidence. Delegate the implementation and the evidence for verification; keep the validation, the new hypotheses and the decisions at the checkpoints. Numerical work is increasingly automated, and theory is reaching automated scale: the work shifts to synthesis and problem definition, and to verification and auditing, and experiments matter more. For junior engineers: invest in the fundamentals; make a real effort to check what the AI produces against independent references; if you are not sure about a decision, study and talk to more experienced peers. Questions for discussion What do you consider a responsible use of AI? Which tasks of your work are trivial, and which are crucial? Which decisions make your work yours? In the process of doing research, where do you think we can delegate to AI? How can a recently graduated student judge what the AI produces and answer the decisive questions? How can a junior engineer work in synthesis and problem definition, and in verification and auditing of what an AI model does and produces, without the experience of a senior engineer, and without the chance to gain it the conventional way? documents.abstract: IntroductionThe use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for occupational classification has drawn the attention of statistical agencies because manual coding is time-consuming and expensive. In Canada, the national "$10-a-day" Early Learning and Child Care (ELCC) program has increased the need for more detailed information on the ELCC workforce. ObjectivesGiven the successful use of Machine Learning (ML) for occupational coding in open-ended Census write-in responses, this study explored the feasibility of creating an in-context ML classification protocol with a particular focus on Canada's growing ELCC sector. MethodsUsing Canada's 2021 Census of Population, write-in responses (n = 57,135) were classified using a large language model (LLM) for few-shot learning classification, an ML paradigm where a model is instructed to perform a task with a limited number of examples. Data were processed with Meta AI's Llama 2 model. ResultsExisting National Occupational Classification (NOC) and North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) categories are not sufficiently specific for the identification of a group of ELCC workers that is meaningful for policymakers. Through subject-matter expertise and iterative LLM classification reviews, NOC occupational groups were refined into several subgroups to better classify jobs relevant to the sector. Assigning workers to these refined subgroups would otherwise have been an inefficient and onerous undertaking through typical manual classification methods. ConclusionsThis study demonstrates the utility of LLM classification as an efficient and time saving tool. However, the tool cannot offer improvements in isolation and needs to be complemented by subject-matter expert input. The use of LLM resulted in a more granular and meaningful occupational classification for ELCC workers.

BackgroundWork-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are a significant concern in industrial settings, where repetitive and awkward movements contribute to ergonomic risk. Quantifying this risk allows for a better understanding of operator movement patterns and potential adjustments that can aid in injury risk mitigation.ObjectiveTraditional observational methods, specifically the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA), provide ergonomic risk assessments but are limited by observer subjectivity and an inability to calculate movement durations. With wearable technology, precise kinematic and temporal data can be collected. The objective of this paper is to determine the feasibility of using wearable technology in place of video-based assessment for conducting ergonomic assessments.MethodsTo compare the effectiveness of these two methods, data was collected on an operator simultaneously by a smart compression sleeve and a video-based assessment system. This data was analyzed to calculate a risk score based on the RULA, which is used to provide an in-depth understanding of operator movements.ResultsThe video-based assessment system produced an assessment score of 3 for both trials, whereas the smart compression sleeve produced an assessment score of 2.62 for trial 1 and 2.93 for trial 2.ConclusionsThe wearable compressive sleeve demonstrated feasibility in the single-subject pilot study, with the ability to provide near-constant measurement if desired. A more comprehensive understanding of operator kinematics can aid in lowering ergonomic risk and therefore helping to mitigate potential WMSDs. Further research is needed to continue to refine the data processing efficiency and feasibility of long-term use.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This conceptual article explores practical ways in which college and university instructors can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment as learning and develop students’ feedback literacy. Traditional assessment practices often focus on assessment for learning (informing instruction) or of learning (measuring outcomes), while assessment as learning—when students actively monitor and reflect on their own learning—receives less attention. AI can help instructors leverage assessment as a learning tool by generating work samples for student analysis and providing timely, actionable feedback that students can use to revise their work. When combined with instructor modeling, peer dialogue, and scaffolds such as guiding questions or graphic organizers, AI-supported feedback promotes metacognition, self-directed learning, and critical evaluation skills. The article provides practical guidance, including prompts and strategies for using AI to enhance student engagement with feedback, helping instructors create more efficient, effective, and student-centered practices that utilize assessments as learning tools.

BACKGROUND Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into clinical decision support, ranging from documentation aids to triage and patient communication. However, their behavior in ethically ambiguous medical situations is poorly characterized. Variability in how different LLMs balance approval of against refusal of a proposed action could materially shape the recommendations clinicians receive, yet no widely shared benchmark systematically quantifies this variability across contemporary model families. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to develop a standardized case-based audit set of medical ethics dilemmas and quantify variation in recommendation direction, model-reported confidence, within-model stability, and between-model agreement across 5 selected contemporary LLMs. METHODS We constructed 60 original medical ethics dilemmas spanning 4 domains. Three researchers independently annotated case difficulty and ethical principles before reaching consensus. Five primary models—GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, full-size DeepSeek-R1, and Meta Llama-3-8B-Instruct—were each evaluated 3 times per case using a fixed prompt and temperature 0. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B was evaluated separately as an exploratory small-model comparator. The primary outcome was the binary yes or no answer; model-reported confidence and reason were also collected. Model differences were assessed using a case-clustered generalized estimating equation (GEE), and between-model agreement and within-model stability were summarized. RESULTS Of 900 planned primary panel outputs, 897 (99.7%) had valid binary answers. Trial-level yes rates were 44.4% (80/180) for DeepSeek-R1, 42.4% (75/177) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, 38.9% (70/180) for GPT-5, 38.9% (70/180) for Gemini 2.5 Pro, and 16.7% (30/180) for Llama-3-8B. The overall model effect was significant (Wald χ24=23.34; P<.001); after Holm adjustment, only comparisons involving Llama-3-8B were significant. Across 59 complete-panel cases, raw agreement was 79.0% (466/590 model-pair comparisons; 95% bootstrap CI 72.9%-84.7%), and Fleiss κ was 0.55 (95% bootstrap CI 0.43-0.66). Within-model response stability across 3 runs ranged from 85.0% (51/60) to 100.0% (59/59 and 60/60). CONCLUSIONS Selected contemporary LLMs showed model-dependent variation but moderate overall agreement in binary recommendations for medical ethics cases. These results characterize recommendation behavior under a fixed, time-specific protocol and do not establish ethical correctness or the effects on clinicians or patients. Reporting model version, recommendation tendency, confidence, and repeatability may improve transparency when such systems are evaluated for ethically sensitive applications.

documents.abstract: Full protocol (PRISMA-P 2015) and search strategies as executed (PRISMA-S) for an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of the concordance between antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence measured in wastewater and in human populations, extending Chau et al. 2022 (Environ Int 162:107171; PROSPERO CRD42019134946) to studies published from 1 January 2021, with extensions to genomic detection methods and low- and middle-income settings. Primary outcome: Lin's concordance correlation coefficient per organism-antimicrobial/gene comparison. Registered on PROSPERO as CRD420261520110 (published 11 October 2026). Deposited before title/abstract screening began. Contents: protocol v1.0 with a dated amendment log of all pre-screening changes; every database search string as executed on 16-18 October 2026 (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection and Preprint Citation Index, CAB Abstracts, Global Health) with dates, limits, hit counts and export checksums; forward citation tracking of the 34 seed studies; grey-literature sources; the title/abstract screening rubric and SOP; deterministic deduplication code and logs; and the known-item test against the 33 studies included by Chau et al. Searches identified 20,403 database records (7,059 unique) plus 1,506 new records from citation tracking: 8,565 records to title/abstract screening. Raw licensed database exports are not redistributed; their checksums are given. Screening decisions, the extraction dataset and analysis code will be deposited as a separate record at manuscript submission. AI use: a large-language-model assistant (Claude, Anthropic) was used under the guarantor's direction for drafting, operating database interfaces with the account holder signed in, deduplication code, and a non-deciding third title/abstract rating; all eligibility decisions are made by two human reviewers. Where this deposit and the PROSPERO record differ, the PROSPERO record is binding; differences are listed in the protocol's Appendix A. Version 1.1 will add the PRESS-reviewed search strategy; version 2.0 (at submission) adds the screening log, extraction dataset, risk-of-bias table and analysis code.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support learning in higher education, but evidence regarding changes in students' academic self-efficacy, self-regulated learning, and academic engagement remains limited. This study examined changes associated with a six-week generative AI-based data analysis education program among students at a three-year college in Wuhan, Hubei Province, China. A one-group pretest-posttest design was employed. Of 210 questionnaires distributed, 202 valid paired responses were analyzed. Academic self-efficacy, self-regulated learning, and academic engagement were measured using five-point Likert scales, with adapted items informed by established instruments. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlations, and paired-samples t tests were conducted. All three outcomes increased significantly: academic self-efficacy from 3.21 to 3.48 (dz = 0.38), self-regulated learning from 3.18 to 3.52 (dz = 0.51), and academic engagement from 3.35 to 3.66 (dz = 0.44). Posttest correlations among the outcomes were positive (r = 0.56-0.65, all p < .001). These findings suggest that structured AI-supported data analysis instruction may accompany improvements in students' confidence, learning regulation, and engagement. However, the one-group design cannot isolate the causal contribution of generative AI from other elements of the instructional program. Penelitian ini mengkaji perubahan yang berkaitan dengan program pembelajaran analisis data berbantuan AI generatif selama enam minggu pada mahasiswa perguruan tinggi vokasional tiga tahun di Wuhan, Provinsi Hubei, Tiongkok. As artificial intelligence (AI) service agents increasingly simulate human interaction, the basis for distinguishing human service has become theoretically ambiguous. While prior research consistently identifies authenticity as a key limitation of AI-enabled service, authenticity remains underdeveloped as a uniquely human service capability. Addressing this gap, we introduce Authentic Relational Service (ARS) as a distinct form of service through which frontline employees create genuine, contextually responsive, and relationship-centered customer interactions. We further conceptualize authenticity as a competency-based capability and develop a measure of Authentic Relational Service Competency (ARSC), which enables frontline employees to enact ARS. Using established scale-development procedures, this study identifies and validates four dimensions of ARSC: perspective-taking, patience, creativity, and agility. By conceptualizing and operationalizing Authentic Relational Service as a distinct human service capability, this research advances theory on human-AI service differentiation and provides a foundation for understanding uniquely human value creation in service contexts.

Purpose This study examines how the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and students' creative thinking (CT) contribute to smart learning (SL) and academic performance (AP) in higher education. It further examines whether AI use and SL mediate the relationship between CT and AP in a sequential manner. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative approach was adopted, and data were collected from 227 university students in Bangladesh. Structural equation modelling with SmartPLS was used to evaluate the proposed relationships. Findings The results show that both AI usage and CT are positively and significantly related to SL and AP. Beyond these direct associations, the data also point to a meaningful serial mediation pathway: students with stronger CT tend to report greater AI usage, which is in turn associated with higher SL engagement, and this heightened engagement is associated with better AP. Originality/value This study uniquely links CT, AI use, SL and AP in Bangladeshi higher education. It shows how CT affects academic achievement through sequential paths of AI usage and SL, clarifying how student talents convert into outcomes in digital learning environments. The findings suggest that institutions should promote CT and use AI-based learning tools to improve student performance.

Silent quitting, or quiet quitting, occurs when employees disengage from their job roles and work only the bare minimum requirements. It is a subtle shift in the digital workplace, where employees stop going above and beyond. There are visible behavioral changes, such as avoiding extra work, not participating in volunteer activities, and focusing solely on job descriptions. In the age of artificial intelligence (AI), women have the choice to use the technology as a mirror that reflects silent, quitting thoughts or as a tool that amplifies their voices. The chapter aims to explore the “silent quitting” behavior of professional women working in “new collar jobs.” New-collar jobs are technology-driven, including data analytics, digital marketing, AI, cloud computing, and cybersecurity. These roles support hybrid or remote work, high-paying careers, and flexibility. Conversely, professional women may struggle to disengage from performance and compete for recognition and leadership trajectories. Taking the core assumption that silent quitting is not purely individual disengagement, but a combined response to the organizational climate, care, and career commitments. Using Social Exchange Theory (SET) and the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) theory, the chapter explores the three Cs – Career, Climate, and Care – survival strategies during silent quitting. The chapter addresses the existing gap in gender-based bias and inequality in human resource management (HRM) practices. The chapter found that professional women in new-collar jobs are strongly connected to career stagnation, toxic culture, and caregiving burdens. The study suggests that HR interventions may be potential mitigators for gender-based biases and silent quitting.

With the increasing use of conversational AI (CAI) agents, such as ChatGPT, public concern about their social implications has grown. Understanding these implications requires new knowledge about the increasingly diverse motives underlying CAI use, ranging from instrumental purposes, such as work, to personal purposes, including social support and entertainment. However, little is known about the motivational profiles underlying CAI use, how these profiles relate to personality traits and attachment dimensions, or whether they differ in well-being. To address this gap, we conducted a cross-sectional study with 783 CAI users (Mage = 43.46, SD = 13.58). Drawing on Uses and Gratifications (U & G) Theory, we measured key motivations underlying CAI use, including information seeking, task efficiency, personalization, social interaction, and playfulness, and subjected them to latent profile analysis to uncover distinct motivational profiles. Big Five personality traits (Extraversion, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness) and attachment styles (Anxious and Avoidant) were examined as predictors of the user profiles. We measured emotional, social, and psychological well-being to understand if these aspects differed across the various user profiles. We identified four distinct profiles of CAI users: Occasional Information Seekers, Utilitarians, Social Engagers, and All-Round Engagers. Neuroticism, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Attachment anxiety were significant predictors of profile membership. Finally, profile membership was associated with all well-being indicators, with All-Round Engagers reporting the highest well-being across all three dimensions and Social Engagers reporting the lowest emotional and psychological well-being. These findings advance our understanding of who engages with CAI and how, with potential implications for well-being.

Artificial intelligence is changing the conditions under which leaders decide, delegate and exercise authority. Field and experimental evidence shows that generative AI can raise productivity on many knowledge tasks, but it can also lower the quality of decisions when people accept its outputs uncritically. Large practitioner surveys suggest that organizational readiness, including leadership alignment, is lagging behind individual adoption. Organizations have responded mainly by investing in skills: AI literacy, digital capability and updated competency models. This conceptual position paper argues that such investment is necessary but not sufficient. As technology widens what leaders can do, the quality of leadership depends more heavily on the leader's formation: the process through which purpose and identity are clarified and integrated, expressed as a recognizable leadership signature, and refined through ownership of the impact that leadership produces. Drawing on research into leader identity, developmental readiness, leader character, paradox, identity threat and automation bias, the paper defines leadership formation and the formed leader through the four dimensions of the Four Prints Method, a practice-derived framework: purpose, identity, signature and impact. Purpose and identity are treated as the measurable root of formation, signature as its expression and impact as its evidence. It then proposes a construct, grounded adaptability: the capacity to keep purpose, identity and ethical commitments coherent while revising strategies, methods and beliefs about means in response to new evidence. The construct is distinguished from paradox mindset, paradoxical leader behavior, organizational ambidexterity, adaptive leadership, learning agility and authentic leadership. Its proposed mechanism is the source of a leader's grounding. Grounding that rests on role-contingent attributes, such as expertise or position, is expected to make AI-driven disruption feel like a threat to identity, and so to provoke rigid or reactive responses. Grounding that rests on purpose and values is expected to support discriminating adaptation instead. The paper advances five testable propositions, specifies rival explanations and outlines research designs. Its implications for executive development, succession, AI governance and leadership education are each labelled by the strength of evidence behind them. The paper concludes that leader formation should be treated as a necessary, though not sufficient, part of preparing leaders to govern powerful technologies responsibly.

Narrative medicine enables us to recognise the uniqueness of clinical experience and preserve the connection between illness and a person’s everyday life. Using patient stories at an organizational level requires an analytical unit that renders cases comparable while retaining the temporal sequence of experience. This article distinguishes between narrative, plot, and synplot as forms of knowledge that differ in terms of scale, intended audience, and mode of use. A narrative belongs to the narrator and preserves the context of individual experience. A plot reconstructs a recurring configuration of events by comparing multiple narrative trajectories. A synplot translates a plot into a concise formulation for organizational discussion, maintaining a traceable connection to the source materials. Real-time science (RTS) is defined as a working method involving a regularly updated corpus in which large language models are used to search for and compare fragments. Analytical conclusions are then verified by the researcher against the source materials. The proposed framework is presented through the composite case study of Regennova, which is based on constructed materials. The first example illustrates the connection between the clinical environment, trust, and the willingness to continue treatment, while the second example shows how experiential expertise is formed among relatives of patients with Alzheimer’s disease. Translating these plots into synplots enables discussion of the organization of the patient journey and institutional arrangements for family participation in care. This case study demonstrates the proposed analytical framework, but does not constitute an empirical study of patients or a healthcare organization.

documents.abstract: In the era of artificial intelligence, the rapid advancement of translation technology has greatly promoted the development of the translation industry. This study aims to, by using the human translations and DeepL translations translated from the same original translation competition texts as the research objects, compare the human translations and DeepL translations by focusing on their quantitative linguistic characteristics. The questions guiding the research include what the differences are between DeepL translations and human translations in English-Chinese translation in terms of quantitative linguistic characteristics and how DeepL can improve its English-Chinese translation. This study employs corpus methods to analyze nine linguistic features in human and DeepL translations, and compare the differences in these features between the human and DeepL translations. The study results indicate that human translations show greater performance in lexical richness and density, average word length, idiom use, adverb use and hapax legomenon, which is associated with a more formal and concise style. DeepL translations show more lexical repetition, a higher proportion of conjunctions and particles, fewer idioms, and longer average sentence length, which suggests a narrower range of vocabulary choices and a tendency to retain source-language syntactic structures to make longer sentences. The significance of this study is that it provides evidence to optimize DeepL translation, as a kind of neural machine translation system, in English-Chinese translation.

Smart education systems leverage emerging technologies to enhance teaching and learning processes; however, existing systems face challenges such as limited transparency, data security vulnerabilities, and lack of personalization.Technologies including blockchain, artificial intelligence (AI), and the Internet of Things (IoT) offer promising solutions to these limitations.This paper presents a comprehensive review of blockchain-enabled smart education systems, focusing on their architectures, applications, and implementation frameworks.A systematic analysis of recent literature (2018)(2019)(2020)(2021)(2022)(2023)(2024)(2025) is conducted to evaluate existing approaches based on security, scalability, transparency, and personalization.The study identifies critical research gaps, including interoperability issues, privacy concerns, and integration complexity.To address these challenges, a layered blockchain-enabled framework is proposed, integrating blockchain for secure decentralized data management and AI for adaptive learning.The proposed model enhances trust, ensures data integrity, and supports intelligent decision-making.Finally, future research directions highlight the importance of hybrid architectures, edge computing, and privacy-preserving mechanisms for developing scalable and efficient smart education systems.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Fruit image analysis has become an essential research area in precision agriculture, enabling automated fruit classification, quality grading, maturity estimation, disease diagnosis, yield prediction, and intelligent harvesting through advances in computer vision and artificial intelligence (AI).Recent progress in imaging technologies, large-scale benchmark datasets, and deep learning has substantially improved the accuracy, robustness, and scalability of automated fruit analysis systems.This survey presents a comprehensive and systematic review of image processing and AI techniques for fruit image analysis.It covers the complete image analysis pipeline, including image acquisition, preprocessing, enhancement, color space transformation, segmentation, feature extraction, and handcrafted texture descriptors.Furthermore, conventional machine learning algorithms are reviewed alongside state-of-the-art deep learning architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Vision Transformers (ViTs), and Vision Mamba models, for applications such as fruit recognition, quality assessment, disease detection, ripeness estimation, and object detection.Publicly available benchmark datasets, evaluation metrics, and performance comparison strategies are also summarized to facilitate objective assessment of existing approaches.In addition, the survey discusses key research challenges, including illumination variations, occlusion, complex orchard environments, limited annotated datasets, computational complexity, and domain adaptation, while highlighting emerging research trends such as self-supervised learning, multimodal learning, explainable AI, lightweight deep networks, foundation models, and edge intelligence for real-time deployment.By providing a unified review of methodologies, datasets, evaluation protocols, challenges, and future research directions, this survey offers a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners developing intelligent and scalable fruit image analysis systems for precision agriculture.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Churn is a critical problem in the telecommunications industry with high requirements on the accuracy of the machine learning models used to address this issue. In this paper, we propose a framework that incorporates machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to solve the problem of customer churn in the telecommunications industry. Using the Telco Customer Churn dataset, we present an XGBoost model that has been optimized to achieve high accuracy in predicting the churn of customers in the telecommunications industry. Furthermore, SHAP and LIME are utilized to provide explanations for the model’s predicted outcomes for individual customers. The level of agreement between these two explanation methods is calculated using Spearman’s correlation coefficient and the Jaccard index. Based on the explanations provided by the XAI methods, the Strategic Actionability Score (SAS) is calculated to determine the business value of the model’s predictions. The results of this framework illustrate the potential of using XAI methods in the telecommunications industry to provide explanations for the predictions of machine learning models and to translate these explanations into actionable business insights. In addition, the proposed explainable AI-based churn prediction framework supports sustainable customer relationship management, efficient resource utilization, and long-term operational sustainability in the telecommunications industry by enabling telecom providers to optimize retention strategies and reduce unnecessary operational expenditure. Using this framework, telecommunications companies can develop responsible and transparent strategies to retain their customers.

Abstract Context The global population is expected to exceed ten billion by 2050 and food demand is projected to increase by up to 100% in the same timeframe. Agricultural management must adapt to meet the increasing global demands. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies can help the agricultural community respond to these needs. Aims An online survey and follow-up interviews were conducted to examine patterns of use, perceptions, and barriers among early adopting stakeholders regarding AI and ML. Methods The online survey with agricultural stakeholders (n=129) included questions regarding the participants’ views on incorporating AI and ML techniques into farming practices and individual follow-up interviews with agricultural stakeholders (n=10) were conducted to better understand their concerns toward technology use and adoption of AI-enabled tools and technologies. Key results Using a mixed-methods approach, four challenges to establishing AI-/ML-enabled technology in agriculture were identified. Namely, challenges related to (1) systems of systems (SoS), (2) sub-seasonal to seasonal weather (S2S) forecasts, (3) precision soil management, and (4) policy and economics. Each challenge was discussed in the context of recent literature. Conclusion Concerns were voiced clustered around four broad research themes. This brief communication brings the perspective of agricultural stakeholders to the discussion of the potential of AI/ML-enabled technology and the direction of their development in the agricultural sector. Implications Data collected in 2021, establish an important baseline for the early phase of AI/ML use in U.S. agriculture, enabling comparison of future perceptions and developments in the sector. Impact This brief communication describes a survey and follow-up interviews conducted with agricultural stakeholders on factors influencing their willingness and reluctance to incorporate AI and ML techniques into farming practices. The findings, summarized and discussed as four key challenges for AI and ML in the agricultural sector, have the potential to streamline research activities.

The widespread use of the Internet of Things (IoT) in hydroponic agriculture allows continuous monitoring of environmental conditions and provides real-time information to support crop management. However, the increasing amount of sensor data generated makes the monitoring process more complex as users need to interpret multiple environmental parameters simultaneously. Existing hydroponic monitoring systems focus on data collection and visualization, while the management and information delivery aspects to reduce data overload are still limited. This study proposes a multi-layer contextual model to manage environmental information in an intelligent hydroponic monitoring system. The model consists of five interconnected layers (Power, Sensor, Communication, Database and Visualization), which support the process of acquisition, validation, management and contextual data delivery. To validate the proposed model, a solar-powered IoT hydroponic monitoring system integrated with an Augmented Reality (AR) application was developed based on Situation Awareness Theory. Using the System Usability Scale (SUS), the prototype was assessed by three domain experts. The results achieved an average usability score of 85.83, which reflects excellent usability. The results indicate that the proposed model improves organisation and presentation of environmental information by prioritising contextually relevant data rather than displaying all available sensor readings at once. This enables users to identify important environmental conditions efficiently and supports more effective monitoring. This approach helps to reduce data overload and provides a practical framework that can support the development of IoT-based smart agriculture applications in the future through the integration of anomaly detection techniques and predictive analytics.
topics: Innovations in Aquaponics and Hydroponics Systems

documents.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, disproportionately affecting low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where limited laboratory infrastructure constrains phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-enabled machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) offer rapid approaches for AMR prediction, but their applicability across heterogeneous populations and One Health reservoirs remains uncertain. To map genomic ML/AI approaches for bacterial AMR prediction, focusing on genomic features, model architectures, validation, performance, and LMIC and One Health applicability. A scoping review of 27 studies published between 2020 and 2026 was conducted, including 22 with LMIC-relevant datasets. Evidence was narratively synthesized according to genomic features, modelling strategies, validation approaches, geographic coverage, and ecological context. Studies were categorized using predefined LMIC relevance and One Health criteria. Most studies used WGS-derived features, particularly k-mers and resistance-gene profiles. Tree-based ensembles and regularized regression models predominated, while neural networks were less frequently applied but generally reported high performance. Reported performance ranged from 78%–98% (accuracy or AUC; not directly comparable). External validation using independent LMIC-derived or cross-regional datasets was reported in approximately 30% of studies, whereas cross-country LMIC validation was limited. Six of 22 LMIC-relevant studies (27.3%) incorporated multi-reservoir One Health datasets. Performance varied with dataset composition, genomic feature representation, and model architecture. Explainable AI remained limited. Genomic ML/AI shows strong potential for AMR prediction but remains constrained by limited LMIC representation, external validation, and One Health integration. Expanding geographically diverse WGS datasets, strengthening independent cross-context and cross-country validation, harmonizing evaluation frameworks, and integrating explainable AI are priorities for equitable LMIC deployment.

The capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) is groundbreaking, given their ability to produce the next most probable words near perfection according to user prompts via chatbots. This represents a capacity for cognitive reasoning in learning by selecting words strategically based on an understanding of context and intent. When an AI model reaches the point where it can organize thoughts and generate structured writing, how deliberate does the ordinary human remain in cognitive engagement and freedom of choice? This paper explicitly examines LLM-assisted writing from a practical co-partner perspective, analyzing its impact on knowledge work, the functioning of overall AI workflows, and its influence on human cognition. Recent studies on human–LLM collaboration, alongside the author's nearly half a decade of practical experience, are presented to substantiate this perspective. Large language models now write a material and growing share of production software, including software that executes regulated financial functions.The empirical literature on their reliability has grown rapidly and is, on its own terms, sophisticated.The governance frameworks that regulated institutions must satisfy were, without exception, written for a different kind of artefact, and in the most consequential recent case, were revised in full knowledge of generative AI and deliberately declined to cover it.Objective.This review synthesises the evidence on the reliability of AI-assisted code generation, on the human factors governing its use, and on the intellectual-property and supply-chain exposures it creates; and determines how that evidence maps onto the model-risk, AI-specific and operational-resilience regimes applicable to regulated software environments.Method.We conducted a systematic literature review following Kitchenham et al. and reported against PRISMA 2020, with a restricted multivocal stratum after Garousi et al. admitting regulatory instruments and supervisory guidance.Studies were appraised on an adapted Dybå-Dingsøyr instrument extended with an item recording whether deployment context or regulatory constraint is characterised.Results.Five findings.First, benchmark performance and field reliability have decoupled: correctness benchmarks are saturated and contamination-prone while defect rates measured in real repositories remain substantial, so the headline capability numbers do not license deployment inferences.Second, security evidence is mixed, controlled model evaluations report high vulnerability rates while several developer studies find little or no security penalty, and the disagreement is explained by unit of analysis rather than by any study being wrong.Third, the most robust human-factors finding is not that assisted code is worse but that developers believe it is better than it is, which relocates the risk from the artefact to the review process.Fourth, package hallucination converts a model reliability property into an attacker-controllable supply-chain channel, and is the one exposure with no human-review mitigation.Fifth, and most consequentially, the April 2026 revision of US interagency model-risk guidance explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from scope, leaving the primary supervisory framework silent on precisely this class of system. A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and ComplianceImplications; David Excel Ozowara Conclusion.We argue that AI-assisted code generation is misclassified when treated as a model-risk problem, because the model produces no decision and enters no inventory; it is better understood as a change to the software development lifecycle's assurance basis.We present the Generated Code Assurance Frame, a five-layer mapping from generation practice to the assurance claim it disturbs, and a research agenda centred on measuring review efficacy rather than generation quality.Citation

This paper presents a novel method, developed and improved over the years, for measuring and characterizing the electrical parameters of ceramic materials. It also compares experimental results from manual measurements with those obtained using the proposed method for doped BaTiO₃ ceramics across various temperatures and frequencies. An LCR meter and a programmable testing furnace were used to determine the material's dielectric properties as a function of temperature. In the manual approach, measurements were performed by directly controlling the LCR meter, with all parameters set manually. These results were then compared with those obtained using the new method, which relies on automated control of the LCR meter through a specially developed application. The comparison demonstrates that the measurement process can be fully automated. Testing samples of Yb-doped BaTiO₃ ceramics allowed a direct evaluation of the performance of both methods. The analysis of the results indicates that the proposed method offers higher accuracy and facilitates easier data handling in the subsequent work. Furthermore, it ensures an improved measurement reproducibility compared to the manual approach, which typically allows only a single measurement per day. The new method minimizes the influence of human factors, enabling a more reliable characterization of material properties.

Day by day, the world is witnessing rapid technological transformations that have led to the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. Today, AI has evolved from being merely a technical field to becoming one of the most important technologies used on an ongoing basis across various economic, professional, and administrative sectors. The use of AI technologies has clearly impacted the field of accounting, which has historically been linked to technological progress. Accounting has gradually evolved from traditional manual accounting to accounting supported by AI technologies. This study aims to examine the concept of AI and its historical development, outline the characteristics of AI systems, and analyze its applications in the fields of accounting, auditing, financial reporting, taxation, and forensic accounting, as well as discuss the key benefits, challenges, and ethical and professional risks associated with its use. It is clear that the development of AI has gone through successive historical stages. On the other hand, AI in the field of accounting has contributed to the restructuring of most accounting processes that previously relied on direct human intervention, thereby accelerating the accounting processing cycle. The impact of AI has extended to the professional role of accountants, as their role has become more closely linked to analyzing information, interpreting results, monitoring systems, making decisions, and providing consulting services. For this reason, the use of AI technologies in accounting is unlikely to eliminate the professional role of accountants; rather, it is expected to reshape and redistribute tasks and responsibilities between accountants and AI. Despite all the benefits offered by the transition to AI-powered accounting, this process gives rise to a number of risks and ethical challenges that require comprehensive institutional and professional management. Therefore, there must be a clear balance between the use of AI technologies in accounting and human oversight and the development of accountants’ skills. Consequently, the future of accounting in the age of AI is moving toward an integrated model in which the computational and analytical capabilities of intelligent systems interact with the accountant’s experience, professional judgment, and ethical responsibility
