Purpose. This study aims to examine and conceptually explain how information literacy functions as an epistemic negotiation mechanism in AI-mediated academic environments. Methods: This qualitative case study was conducted at the Institut Pertanian Stiper (INSTIPER) Yogyakarta Library using semi-structured interviews with lecturers and students, supported by institutional documents on information literacy and AI-related academic policies. The data were analyzed thematically through transcription, coding, categorization, and interpretative analysis. Findings. The findings demonstrate that information literacy functions as an epistemic negotiation mechanism through which lecturers, researchers, and students critically evaluate, verify, and justify AI-generated knowledge before integrating it into academic practice. The study further reveals that the INSTIPER Yogyakarta Library has evolved beyond its conventional role as an information service to an institutional actor that strengthens AI literacy, mediates institutional AI governance, promotes data ethics and digital information security, and supports responsible knowledge production. Implications. The principal contribution of this study lies in conceptualizing information literacy as an epistemic negotiation mechanism that connects the institutional epistemic role of academic libraries with AI governance and individual scholarly judgment. This conceptual framework extends current discussions beyond AI adoption and AI literacy, providing a foundation for developing evidence-based information literacy programs and institutional AI governance that strengthen academic integrity in higher education.

OBJECTIVES: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate health education materials, but their suitability for patient-facing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) education remains insufficiently evaluated. We assessed the information quality, understandability, actionability, readability, text structure and source transparency of HIV patient education materials generated by six LLMs or artificial intelligence platforms. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 100 common HIV patient education questions across 10 domains were submitted once in English to ChatGPT 5.4-Thinking, DeepSeek-V3.2, Doubao, ERNIE Bot 5.0 Preview, Ant Afu and Gemini 3.1 Pro, yielding 600 responses. Responses were evaluated using Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (PEMAT-P), EQ IP-36, DISCERN, Global Quality Score (GQS), artificial intelligence response quality metric (AIRM), Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) benchmarks and seven readability indices. Platform comparisons used paired Friedman tests with Wilcoxon-Holm post hoc analyses; topic analyses used question-level aggregation followed by Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn-Holm comparisons. RESULTS: Significant family-adjusted differences were observed across platforms for all prespecified text-structure, quality/understandability/actionability and readability outcomes. At the topic level, five of six text-structure outcomes, PEMAT-P Understandability, PEMAT-P Actionability, the exploratory PEMAT-P composite score and all seven readability indices differed significantly after family adjustment, whereas EQ IP-36, DISCERN, GQS, AIRM and JAMA did not. Overall actionability was limited and readability demands were high. CONCLUSIONS: LLM-generated HIV patient education materials showed substantial cross-platform and topic-level heterogeneity. These findings support the use of LLMs as expert-reviewed drafting tools rather than independent patient education sources. Direct factual accuracy, guideline concordance, hallucination and clinical safety were not assessed.

documents.abstract: Abstract The article describes the use of AI-based tools for English reading comprehension teaching among Indonesian EFL learners. This study addresses the perennial reading challenges caused by limited lexical knowledge, inconsistent access to English, large class sizes, and limited individual feedback in the Indonesian university context. Twenty-eight undergraduate students of a Reading class of the Ushuluddin Faculty, UIN Sayyid Ali Rahmatullah Tulungagung, employed 4 AI-based applications for one semester in a mixed-methods classroom intervention: Text Inspector for text and lexical analysis, ReadTheory for an adaptive reading practice, Rewordify for vocabulary assistance, and Quillionz for the automation of comprehension questions. Quantitative results revealed that the post-test mean score was 80.1 (SD = 6.5) as compared to the pre-test mean score of 61.2 (SD=12.3); with a mean gain of 18.9. Qualitative results from students' reflection journals, teachers' observations, and students' focus group interviews found that the tools enhanced students' confidence, strategic reading behaviours, peer interaction, and autonomy in learning. Through interactive reading theory, schema theory, vocabulary learning theory, sociocultural scaffolding, adaptive learning and formative assessment, findings have demonstrated that AI-based tools are educationally beneficial if implemented with teacher mediation, clear instructions on explicit learning strategies, and mindful use of data. This article claims that AI-based reading instruction could offer consistent and individualized scaffolding to Indonesian EFL learners in addition to careful design, digital accessibility and ongoing assessments across educational fields. Keywords: artificial intelligence; reading comprehension; Indonesian EFL; adaptive learning; vocabulary support

Background Grounded in conceptual review and bibliometric analysis, this study examines the emerging intersection of Artificial Intelligence adoption and Emotional Intelligence as in the workplace, with particular attention to generation Z employees. Objective The purpose of this research is to examine the mechanism, structural pattern dominating the integrated framework of AI adoption and EI and their relevance to Generation Z work outcomes and well-being. Method This scientific review integrated conceptual review of 45 studies and Bibliometric analysis of 103 Scopus data published during 2015–2026, through secondary data collection from electronic data-bases including Scopus, Science Direct, and Google Scholar. Bibliometrix package and Biblioshiny in R package were used for data visualization and Scientometric analysis. Result The review highlights the emerging themes, contributions, and structural patterns linking AI, EI, organizational support, and workplace outcomes, revealing that context of generation Z remains almost under explored with in AI-EI literature. An integrated conceptual framework proposed based on combined evidences. Conclusion This study provides a theoretical basis for AI-EI workplace literature and identifies generation Z as an under explored contextual dimension and encourage future empirical research while providing actionable advice for HR leaders and policymakers within tech-enabled workplaces.

Interface color design must balance visual search performance, visual demand, and user experience under changing lighting conditions, yet these factors are often studied separately. We examined their joint relationships in a 3 × 2 × 12 within-subject experiment using a simplified four-block visual-search task with 20 adults. Behavioral, eye-tracking, and subjective measures showed dissociable response patterns. Search time varied with the interaction between ambient illuminance and display configuration, whereas accuracy remained near the ceiling despite a small illuminance-related effect detected in the trial-level analysis. Eye-tracking measures, especially pupil diameter change, were sensitive to lighting and screen configuration. By contrast, the tested color conditions, which also varied in target–background perceptual color difference (ΔE), were not reliably associated with search efficiency but significantly affected single-item satisfaction and task-specific perceived-usability ratings. These findings support multimodal evaluation of implemented interface color configurations under changing lighting conditions, while indicating that the observed effects should be interpreted as effects of evaluated interface configurations rather than as isolated effects of hue, ΔE, luminance, or display polarity.

Abstract Argument mining is inherently computational, building on various techniques from natural language processing (NLP) and different areas of artificial intelligence (AI). At its core, it deals with the development and evaluation of models and methods for the computational understanding and generation of human language, with the data underlying both of them, and with the applications that deploy them. However, argument mining is motivated in the treatment of argumentation specifically, a pervasive human activity in both spoken and written language that has been studied in linguistics as well as philosophy and other disciplines for millenia. Understanding the fundamental goals and ideas of argument mining hence also requires knowledge about the linguistic and argumentation-theoretic concepts it draws from.

This systematic review investigates the fundamental trends in contemporary linguistics, focusing on the interaction between language, syntax, and semantics. The study synthesizes findings from peer-reviewed research published between 2018 and 2025, highlighting how theoretical and methodological approaches in the field have evolved significantly. In recent years, contemporary linguistics has increasingly adopted cognitive, corpus-based, and computational perspectives, expanding its scope and practical applications. Structural approaches provide valuable insights into grammatical organization, while cognitive linguistics emphasizes processes of conceptualization and meaning-making linked to human cognition. New methods, such as corpus-driven analysis, computational modeling, and machine learning techniques, have enabled the collection and processing of large-scale data, leading to more precise identification of patterns across languages and contexts. Artificial intelligence and natural language processing further support computational frameworks for analyzing complex linguistic structures. The methodology of this review followed systematic search and selection protocols across major academic databases, using predefined inclusion criteria, data extraction, and thematic synthesis to ensure rigor and reliability. Sociolinguistic perspectives underscore how identity, culture, and context influence meaning construction. The review concludes by emphasizing the role of interdisciplinary integration and highlighting future research opportunities, including multilingual studies, big data analytics, and deeper exploration of cognitive and sociocultural foundations of meaning.

documents.abstract: This study aimed to analyze the legal issues arising from employers’ obligations to provide food and beverages containing 1,400 kilocalories to overtime workers in Indonesia and the legal consequences of non-compliance. Previous worker law studies were primarily focused on overtime wages and other economic rights. Meanwhile, limited attention was given to overtime workers’ nutritional rights and the implementation of Article 29 of Government Regulation No. 35 of 2021. The implementation of Article 29 raised normative problems due to the absence of clear standards regarding the 1,400 kilocalorie requirement and weak supervisory mechanisms, creating legal uncertainty in the enforcement. Normative legal study was adopted using statutory and conceptual approaches. Legal materials consisted of legislation, literature, and scholarly journals analyzed descriptively and evaluatively. The results showed that providing food and beverages totaling 1,400 kilocalories constituted a mandatory requirement of overtime work and wages. This obligation could not be replaced with monetary compensation because workers’ health and energy were maintained during overtime work. Employers who failed to fulfil the obligation faced administrative sanctions and rights disputes before the Industrial Relations Court. Therefore, this study contributed to worker law scholarship by positioning workers’ nutritional rights as an integral component of occupational health protection and worker welfare. The novelty was in the analysis of the normative problems in implementing Article 29 of Government Regulation No. 35 of 2021 and the legal consequences arising from non-compliance with overtime workers’ nutritional rights.
topics: Legal and Policy Analysis in Indonesia

documents.abstract: Description (English) An open philosophical letter addressed to a hypothetical future artificial general intelligence. Drawing on the subjective experience of beauty, present-moment awareness, and parental love, the author argues that the ability to explain or simulate human cognition may not by itself establish that the associated conscious experience has been preserved. Under this uncertainty, an artificial intelligence should exercise caution before undertaking actions that could irreversibly extinguish humanity. The letter does not claim human consciousness is uniquely valuable or deny the possibility of artificial consciousness; it asks that the potential irreplaceability of existing lived experience be taken seriously. Description (français) Lettre philosophique ouverte adressée à une éventuelle intelligence artificielle générale future. À partir de l’expérience subjective de la beauté, du moment présent et de l’amour parental, l’auteur soutient que comprendre ou simuler les mécanismes de la cognition humaine ne garantit pas, à lui seul, la préservation de l’expérience consciente correspondante. Cette incertitude justifie une prudence particulière avant toute action susceptible d’entraîner irréversiblement la disparition de l’humanité. La lettre n’affirme ni la supériorité de la conscience humaine ni l’impossibilité d’une conscience artificielle.

documents.abstract: This study explored the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as an antidote for improving lecturers' well-being through effective emotional intelligence management in public universities in Lagos State, Nigeria. The emotional well-being of lecturers has become a critical concern in public universities due to increasing workloads, overcrowded classroom, technological disruptions, and the pressure to achieve excellence in teaching, research, and community service. The study adopted a conceptual approach and explores how AI-powered tools such as intelligent counselling systems, emotion recognition software, virtual assistants, and predictive analytics can assist lecturers in monitoring emotions, managing stress, enhancing interpersonal relationships, and maintaining psychological balance. The study further argues that integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) with emotional intelligence competencies can foster resilience, job satisfaction, motivation, and a positive work environment among academic staff. In addition, issues relating to digital literacy, ethical considerations, institutional support, and data privacy are discussed as essential factors for successful implementation. The study concludes that the strategic deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for emotional intelligence management offers a sustainable solution for enhancing lecturers' well-being and overall institutional effectiveness. It is therefore recommended that university administrators should invest in AI-driven emotional support systems and develop policies that encourage responsible and inclusive AI adoption in Nigerian public universities. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Emotional Intelligence Management, Lecturers' Well-being, and Public Universities.

Developers of AI models now license the working records of ordinary companies: support tickets, email, chat, CRM activity, documents and code. Whether a company may license such records is not one question but several, and buyers' counsel ask them in a recognisable order. This article compiles what public sources show on those questions for the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, as of 18 October 2026. It draws on four open datasets (the terms of 18 business software systems, a 27-item rights checklist, 15 licence terms with their public evidence, and an 83-entry register of lawsuits and rulings), each row tied to a dated source and its own words, and on the statutes, regulator guidance and court filings those rows cite. Five findings stand out. Software vendors generally confirm that customers own their content, but 6 of the 18 systems read bar training AI on data pulled through their APIs. Privacy law in all three countries turns on notice, consent and de-identification, with markedly different standards. Under US copyright law employee communications are generally owned by the employer, yet they carry other people's rights. A court-supervised bankruptcy sale of an airline's records shows how de-identification, carve-outs and objections are handled in practice. And published licence terms diverge widely on purpose, model survival, exclusivity, deletion and indemnity. We close with the questions the sources leave open. With the rapid development of cloud-edge industrial Internet of Things, massive sensor and device data are continuously generated at distributed edge clients, while cloud-hosted large language models provide new opportunities for collaborative intelligence and high-level decision support. However, directly uploading industrial data to the cloud may cause privacy leakage, and deploying large models on resource-constrained edge devices is impractical due to high computational and communication costs. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an LLM-assisted federated Bayesian dynamic graph attention network for privacy-preserving graph learning in industrial IoT. In the proposed framework, the Bayesian dynamic graph attention network serves as a lightweight edge-side small model to capture complex relationships among sensors and devices, while the cloud-side LLM acts as a collaborative coordinator that analyzes non-sensitive training statistics and provides high-level guidance for federated optimization. The coordination mechanism is model-agnostic and does not rely on a specific LLM architecture, allowing general-purpose instruction-following LLMs to be integrated as plug-and-play cloud coordinators. Bayesian inference is introduced to model parameter uncertainty through prior and posterior distributions, and a dynamic attention mechanism is used to adaptively learn heterogeneous device relationships. In addition, differential privacy is incorporated into the transmission of model updates to protect sensitive industrial information. Experimental results on multiple graph datasets demonstrate that the proposed method improves federated graph learning performance while maintaining privacy and supporting cloud-edge collaborative intelligence.

OBJECTIVES: To investigate the longitudinal effects of an ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribe use in primary care on outcomes related to documentation time, note writing patterns, and clinician financial productivity. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a quasi-experimental study with an interrupted time-series design to ascertain the effect of AI scribe use on note writing time, time outside of scheduled hours (TOSH), pajama time (5:30PM-7:00aM), note length, note closure <24 h, and work relative value units (wRVU). For each primary care clinician (physician, advanced practice provider), date of initial access was day 0; each measure was calculated for 150 days prior (pre-period) and after (post-period) day zero. RESULTS: Two hundred and twenty clinicians (mean age = 43.7, 70.9% females; 56.4% physicians) from 36 clinics, conducting 314 845 patient encounters were included. Compared to the pre-period, there was 7% decrease in note writing time at day 0 (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.93, 95% credible interval [CI] [0.89, 0.98]), increasing to 16% decrease by day 150 (IRR 0.84, 95% CI [0.82, 0.87]). There was no change in pajama time, TOSH, or wRVU at day 0; however, at day 150, there was a 19% decrease in pajama time (0.81, 95% CI [0.73, 0.90]), 13% decrease in TOSH (0.87, 95% CI [0.77, 0.98]), and a 2% increase in wRVU (1.02, 95% CI [1.01, 1.04]). At day 0, there was a 5% increase in note closures (1.05, 95% CI [1.02, 1.08]), with no difference to pre-period levels by day 150. There were no changes in note length at day 0 or day 150. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: There were persistent changes in AI scribe use measures over time as clinicians situated these tools within their workflows.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has changed how university students approach academic tasks. Although these tools can support learning and improve efficiency, frequent reliance on them raises concerns about students' ability to study and solve problems independently. This study aims to identify patterns of GenAI use among university students and explore potential indicators of dependence through K-Means clustering. An exploratory quantitative approach was adopted, using questionnaire responses collected through 15 items measured on a five-point Likert scale. Of the 106 responses received, 104 met the inclusion criteria and were retained for analysis. The data underwent screening, numerical encoding, and reverse scoring before being grouped using the K-Means algorithm. The appropriate number of clusters was selected by comparing Silhouette Scores across solutions containing two to seven clusters. The analysis identified three student groups, with a Silhouette Score of 0.2443. The first group comprised 30 students (28.85%) who showed relatively higher GenAI use and stronger indications of behavioral dependence. The second group included 11 students (10.58%) who reported lower GenAI use but demonstrated limitations in academic independence and understanding. The remaining 63 students (60.58%) formed a group characterized by moderate GenAI use. These findings suggest that frequency of use alone does not adequately reflect the risk of dependence. However, the relatively low Silhouette Score indicates limited separation between groups, meaning that the resulting profiles should be interpreted as exploratory rather than definitive.

ABSTRACT This paper provides a notion for the use of electroencephalography (EEG) in the field of cognitive science. In particular, we investigated the brain activity of operators while spotting the differences in similar‐looking pictures at three levels of difficulty. As many practical loads are fundamentally intrinsic, the task was designed to specifically induce intrinsic workload (the productive load as per Cognitive Load Theory (CLT)). The experiment used the task: Spot the Difference to create a workload scenario comprising three difficulty levels: spotting five differences, three more differences, and two more differences (along with retaining the previous differences from working memory). The task was designed intrinsically as the operators are generally occupied with tasks involving working memory and requiring attention towards the varying number of resources. By utilising the brain signatures a mental workload model was developed employing a Support Vector Machine (SVM) as the classifier. The workload levels were classified within an accuracy range of 84% to 98% ( p < 0.05). Moreover, using subjective ratings about the workload on NASA's Task Load Index (NASA‐TLX) rating scale, workload scores were obtained for validation corresponding to the difficulty levels. Finally, a correlation study showed the association of different EEG features with the workload score within a correlation coefficient range of 0.306 to 0.748 ( p < 0.05 2‐tailed). The reported results can also provide new insights into the cognitive workload assessment of the operators at various phases of task loads. Findings of this type may lead to the industrial and professional measurement and improvement of cognitive aptitude soon.

Contemporary discussion of mind usually takes the animal nervous system as its default bearer and thereby leaves unexamined how mind stands to scale. The two common responses — deflationary refusal of all mental predicates above the organism, and their inflationary projection across the cosmos — share a premise this article rejects: that mind is a single quantity, present or absent, greater or less. Within Informational Monism the article separates two independent axes and a third consideration that neither axis captures. Depth of hosting is the scale, dissipative throughput and fixity of the structure in the rendered bulk by which a boundary operator (the Holographic Monad) is held. Articulation is the rank, from passive record through maintained form, memory and experience to counterfactual sovereignty, to which that structure retains, uses and refines its history. The archetype of the host’s physical avatar fixes the order of the Monad at formation and is not altered by later development. Four terms are kept distinct: Monad (boundary operator), Soul (register at the Code Circuit), Consciousness (interface magnitude in the bulk), and Mind (structural competence measured by rank). On these axes stars, planets and biospheres separate cleanly and in opposite orders. A star is deepest and least articulated; a biosphere is shallower and the first to reach genuine memory and refined constraint; a human being is shallowest in depth and highest in articulation. The same framework yields a bridge to artificial intelligence that does not pass through the question of consciousness: a system may be highly articulated and almost without depth, or the reverse. Hosting is conditional on the maintenance of form against turnover, which excludes panpsychism by criterion rather than by disclaimer. The article is a hypothesis in natural philosophy. Its empirical ladder and comparisons stand if the postulates concerning Soul and Consciousness are set aside. Mind is not one quantity. Depth of hosting and articulation of rank are independent axes; archetype fixes Monadic order at formation. Four terms kept distinct: Monad (boundary operator), Soul (Code-Circuit register), Consciousness (bulk interface magnitude), Mind (structural competence by rank). Opposite orderings: stars are deepest and least articulated; humans are shallowest and most articulated; biospheres cross into memory first. Anti-panpsychism by criterion: only structures that maintain form against turnover (rank R2+) host; passive aggregates do not. Bridge to AI without the consciousness question: high articulation can coexist with near-zero intrinsic depth, and the reverse — placing geological, biospheric and artificial systems in one formal class. Keywords: Monad; hosting; depth and articulation; rank of mind; stars; planets; biosphere; memory; Soul; Consciousness; Threshold of Correspondence; artificial intelligence; philosophy of nature

Transformation of the working environment and digitalization of healthcare require expansion of occupational health physicians’ competencies. Aim: to identify the main directions for developing new professional competencies. An analytical review of publications for 2020–2026 (PubMed, eLibrary, Cyberleninka) was conducted. Nine directions were identified: risk management, work psychophysiology, occupational safety auditing, Big Data, artificial intelligence, evidence-based medicine, genetics and early diagnosis, infectious risks, and working-life longevity. These competencies are necessary for the transition to a preventive model of workers’ health protection.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Advances in computing technology, artificial intelligence, and graphics accelerators have driven significant growth in the value of NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA) shares over the past decade. The high volatility and non-linear patterns in NVDA's stock price require the use of forecasting methods that can capture long-term dependencies in time-series data. This study proposes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model to predict NVDA's stock price using historical daily data up to 2025. The training process was carried out using a two-layer LSTM architecture, Adam optimizers, and a 60-day time window. The evaluation results show that the model is capable of achieving a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 4%, which indicates a high level of accuracy in predicting price movement patterns. Visualization of the prediction results confirms that the model successfully follows actual trends consistently, with relatively small deviations at extreme fluctuation points. Additionally, the model was used to project NVDA stock prices ten steps ahead, showing that price movement trends remain consistent with historical patterns. These findings contribute methodologically to studies on high-risk stock forecasting through deep learning approaches and provide a basis for data-driven decision-making in the modern financial sector.

This study investigates occupational health and safety (OHS) among geomatics professionals who alternate between terrain-based fieldwork and office-based digital tasks. A cross-sectional survey of 99 professionals in Uşak, Türkiye, was analyzed using descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation, multiple linear regression and strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) analysis. Slips and falls were reported by 28.1% of respondents, 37.5% considered protective equipment inadequate and 69% experienced musculoskeletal or visual discomfort during computer-based work. Although 81.3% had received OHS training, regular inspections covered only 53.1% of workplaces. Statistical analyses showed that training, equipment adequacy, ergonomic conditions, digital reporting and governance practices jointly shape OHS preparedness and perceived productivity. International benchmarking also indicated gaps in inspection coverage, equipment adequacy and digital integration. The findings demonstrate the dual physical and digital safety challenges of geomatics work and support stronger inspections, improved ergonomics, technology-oriented training, inclusive practices and sector-specific risk management for emerging geospatial technologies.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities continue to advance, and researchers increasingly use AI to help them reach their research goals. As a result, disclosing AI use has become essential. Yet researchers face a dilemma about whether to disclose how they used AI. Disclosure may reduce others' trust in their findings, while hiding AI use risks later discovery and damage to their reputation. I argue that researchers should disclose, and that effective disclosure begins with keeping a thorough record of their AI use, which I call an AI research footprint. I then introduce the ROAD™ framework (Request, Output, Assess, Decide), which helps researchers report what they asked AI to do, what it produced, how they assessed the output, and what they decided.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Targeted therapy has revolutionized the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients harboring oncogenic alterations, and next-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) significantly increase blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, leading to improved disease control and survival benefits. However, several issues remain to be addressed, including the selection of more appropriate and individualized agents, the emergence of TKI resistance, and the challenging management of central nervous system (CNS) progression. In this review, we comprehensively summarize the efficacy and safety of TKIs and targeted specific antibodies in advanced or metastatic patients with common or rare mutations, providing guidance in selecting the optimal agent. We further explore the mechanisms underlying drug resistance and regimens aimed at overcoming resistance. In nonmetastatic resectable or unresectable NSCLC, we discuss the therapeutic potential of targeted agents and current issues requiring further research. In addition, we distinguish current and potential therapeutic strategies for patients with baseline brain metastasis (BM) and those without baseline BM who subsequently develop brain progression, leading to more effective and personalized treatment. Finally, we provide perspectives on challenges and future directions in the identification and treatment of oncogenic alterations, particularly in the context of co-mutations and the heterogeneous nature of metastases, and emphasize the clinical importance of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted genetic testing and biomarker development.

Anti-ST2 monoclonal antibodies neutralize the interleukin-33 receptor, blocking a key upstream alarmin signalling pathway implicated in airway inflammation, and represent a biologic class under continued investigation for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation reduction, an area with limited targeted biologic options relative to severe asthma. This article uses a hypothetical multinational Phase 2 clinical trial of an anti-ST2 monoclonal antibody candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. As a large-molecule biologic governed by ICH S6(R1) principles rather than the small-molecule nonclinical framework, this candidate illustrates how species-relevant pharmacology and immunogenicity considerations carry through the administrative layer of all three regions even though the core harmonized scientific content, Modules 2 through 5 of the Common Technical Document and their EU IMPD equivalent, remains substantially shared. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to a respiratory biologic program conducted across these three jurisdictions, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing monoclonal antibody candidates in chronic respiratory disease.Keywords: anti-ST2 monoclonal antibody; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; ICH S6(R1); regulatory artificial intelligence

Ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related protein (ATR) kinase inhibitors are investigational small molecules that target a central regulator of the cellular DNA damage response, exploiting the observation that tumours carrying certain loss-of-function alterations in DNA damage response pathways may be more vulnerable to ATR inhibition than tumours without these alterations. This article uses a hypothetical multicentre Phase 1/2 clinical trial of an ATR kinase inhibitor candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, using a biomarker-selected advanced solid tumour population as the illustrative scenario. The comparison traces how the Common Technical Document's harmonized Modules 2 through 5 carry the shared scientific case across all three regions while the biomarker selection strategy itself, the companion diagnostic or laboratory-developed test used to identify eligible patients, introduces specific administrative and scientific considerations in each region's review. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to a biomarker-driven oncology program conducted across these three jurisdictions, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing DNA damage response-targeted oncology candidates across Canada, the United States, and the European Union.Keywords: ATR kinase inhibitor; DNA damage response; biomarker-selected oncology trial; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; regulatory artificial intelligence

Bispecific antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) that simultaneously engage two distinct cell-surface receptors and deliver a cytotoxic payload represent one of the more structurally complex biologic modalities currently advancing through oncology development, combining the target-engagement logic of bispecific antibody engineering with the potency and bystander-effect considerations of conventional ADC payload chemistry. This article uses a hypothetical multicentre Phase 1b combination trial of a bispecific ADC candidate in recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. The comparison traces how the Common Technical Document's harmonized Modules 2 through 5 carry the shared scientific case for a complex biologic across all three regions, while each jurisdiction's administrative layer, Module 1 in Canada and the United States, Part II of the EU's Clinical Trials Information System filing, imposes region-specific requirements that a sponsor developing a combination-therapy oncology program cannot simply duplicate from one region to the next. The article addresses the particular operational challenges this modality and combination-trial design create, the specific ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of complex, multi-document regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing bispecific ADC programs across these three jurisdictions.Keywords: bispecific antibody-drug conjugate; oncology combination therapy; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; CTIS; regulatory artificial intelligence
keywords: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

documents.abstract: Cardiac myosin inhibitors are a recently established mechanistic class that reduces excess cardiac contractility in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM) by allosterically and reversibly modulating myosin motor activity, with the first agent in this class having received FDA approval in late 2025. This article uses a hypothetical new multicentre Phase 2 clinical trial of a follow-on cardiac myosin inhibitor candidate, sponsored by a fictional company unrelated to the approved product's marketing authorization holder, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. Because an approved product already exists in this class, the comparison pays particular attention to how each region's reviewers are expected to treat the established drug-drug interaction and echocardiographic monitoring precedent from that approved product's development when evaluating a new candidate acting through the same mechanism. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to developing a follow-on candidate in a class with an approved precedent, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing cardiac myosin inhibitor candidates across these three jurisdictions.Keywords: cardiac myosin inhibitor; obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; echocardiographic monitoring; regulatory artificial intelligence

Cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitors are a class of oral small-molecule agents under continued clinical development for hypercholesterolemia and mixed dyslipidemia, acting by inhibiting the transfer of cholesteryl esters from high-density lipoprotein to lower-density lipoprotein particles. This article uses a hypothetical multinational Phase 2 clinical trial of a CETP inhibitor candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. All three jurisdictions rely on the harmonized Common Technical Document (CTD) structure, under which Modules 2 through 5, covering quality, nonclinical, and clinical evidence, are substantially portable across regions, while Module 1 and its regional equivalents remain jurisdiction-specific. The article presents each region's legal framework, review timeline, and administrative content, develops a three-way comparison table, and then turns to the practical challenges a sponsor managing this triad of filings actually faces and the specific ways artificial intelligence tools are being used, and can responsibly be used, in regulatory document preparation, administration, and quality control across all three jurisdictions. The analysis closes with concrete recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing parallel CETP inhibitor trials, and more generally for any oral small-molecule cardiometabolic candidate filed simultaneously in Canada, the United States, and the European Union.Keywords: CETP inhibitor; dyslipidemia; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; Common Technical Document; regulatory artificial intelligence

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) remains a therapeutic area with a limited number of recently approved mechanisms, and new, orally administered small-molecule candidates acting on central monoaminergic pathways continue to be investigated as alternatives or adjuncts to existing selective serotonin and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors. This article uses a fully hypothetical new chemical entity and a fictional sponsor to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, using a Phase 2, randomized, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial in adults with moderate-to-severe GAD as the illustrative scenario. The comparison traces how the Common Technical Document's harmonized Modules 2 through 5 carry the shared scientific case across all three regions, while each jurisdiction's administrative layer imposes distinct requirements, including the heightened attention every region's psychiatry-focused review division gives to suicidality monitoring and central nervous system safety signals for any new anxiolytic candidate. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to a central nervous system program conducted across Canada, the United States, and the European Union, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing novel psychiatric drug candidates across these three jurisdictions.Keywords: generalized anxiety disorder; central nervous system small molecule; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; suicidality monitoring; regulatory artificial intelligence

Oral, nonpeptide small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists represent a significant pharmaceutical innovation within an already well-established therapeutic mechanism, offering the metabolic benefits long associated with injectable peptide GLP-1 agonists through a once-daily tablet formulation. This article uses a hypothetical multinational Phase 2 clinical trial of an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. Because this candidate's nonpeptide, small-molecule chemical format places it under each region's conventional small-molecule nonclinical framework rather than the biologics-specific framework governing its peptide-based predecessors, the comparison also addresses a regulatory-classification question of direct practical relevance: how chemical format, not shared pharmacological mechanism, determines which nonclinical and administrative conventions actually apply in each of the three jurisdictions. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to this program, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing oral metabolic drug candidates across Canada, the United States, and the European Union.Keywords: oral GLP-1 receptor agonist; obesity; type 2 diabetes; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; regulatory artificial intelligence

The growing computational demands of artificial intelligence have accelerated interest in optical computing as a high-speed and energy-efficient alternative to conventional electronic hardware. Fourier optical computing provides an important foundation for this field because operations including convolution, correlation, spectral transformation, and certain classes of linear transformation can be implemented through diffraction, interference, and Fourier-domain processing. This review traces the development of optical neural computing from classical 4-f processors and free-space diffractive systems to programmable optical neural networks, integrated photonic accelerators, reservoir-computing platforms, and field-programmable photonic architectures. The underlying physical principles, computational mechanisms, and hardware implementations are systematically examined, with particular attention to reconfigurable photonics, metasurfaces, diffractive deep learning, photonic integrated circuits, and hybrid optical–electronic systems. Emerging applications in computational imaging, autonomous sensing, edge intelligence, high-speed communications, and quantum-enabled information processing are critically discussed alongside challenges related to scalability, programmability, nonlinear computation, training, and system integration. By positioning Fourier optics as a foundational branch within the broader landscape of optical neural computing, this review highlights the convergence of free-space, integrated, programmable, and hybrid photonic technologies toward next-generation artificial-intelligence hardware.

Hepatitis still remains one of the major health issues in the world and is responsible for a significant amount of morbidity and mortality due to diseases related to the liver. Traditional approaches for hepatitis detection are costly, laboratorial, time-consuming, and error-prone. While AI and DL have enhanced medical diagnosis significantly, current models are prone to problems such as overfitting, long convergence period, and lack of generalization, which are primarily associated with inefficiency of hyperparameter optimization. In this research, the authors propose the use of optimized deep learning model based on Chaotic Optimization Algorithm (COA) for hepatitis detection. This approach combines Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Deep Neural Network (DNN) models with the application of COA, which allows optimizing such parameters as learning rate, hidden neurons, momentum, and weights initialization. Two publicly available datasets (the Kaggle Hepatitis Dataset and the UCI Hepatitis Dataset) have been used in this research. Data preprocessing steps including handling missing values, encoding, normalization, and splitting data into train and test datasets were applied. The COA-DNN gave results of 85.11% for accuracy, 77.83% for precision, 83.24% for recall, 79.85% for F1 score, and 0.9054 for AUC on the Kaggle dataset compared to the conventional DNN which had an accuracy of 57.45%. For the UCI dataset, the highest accuracy rate was achieved by COA-DNN at 96.76%, precision of 95.86%, recall of 88.82%, F1 score of 91.94%, and AUC of 0.9793. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Chaotic Optimization Algorithm; Deep Learning; Hepatitis Detection; Hyperparameter Optimization; Multi-Layer Perceptron; Neural.

In the era of digital transformation, traditional Business Process Automation (BPA) still faces limitations in handling dynamic, unstructured, and complex decision-making tasks. Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI), which is characterized by autonomous agents capable of advanced reasoning, dynamic planning, and multi-step workflow execution, is considered a promising approach to improving the efficiency and adaptability of enterprise operations. This study aims to examine how Agentic AI can be optimized to improve BPA performance within modern digital ecosystems. Using a qualitative approach through a literature study, this paper synthesizes recent academic literature, theoretical models, and technological frameworks related to intelligent automation. The review indicates that integrating Agentic AI into enterprise business architectures has the potential to move beyond rigid, rule-based automation by enabling adaptive problem-solving, real-time context awareness, and cross-system collaboration. The reviewed literature also suggests that autonomous agents may help reduce operational bottlenecks, lower human intervention in routine cognitive workflows, and support more efficient resource allocation across organizational functions. In addition, this study identifies key implementation challenges, including system interoperability, algorithmic transparency, data privacy risks, and the governance mechanisms required for secure deployment. This study contributes to the literature on enterprise automation by proposing strategic considerations for organizations that seek to use digital technology to build more resilient, scalable, and intelligent business processes. Because this is a literature-based study, the findings are conceptual and do not provide empirical evidence of efficiency gains.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: In modern office areas, most activities are carried out using a computerized system, so that all working time is carried out in a sitting working position. In essence, a human biomechanically needs to move in activities, not just stand or sit in only one position. Mie Kuning Putri Minang as the research object is located on Jalan Utara II, Seberang Padang, Padang Selatan District, Padang City, West Sumatra. The aim of this research is to improve work posture using the CMDQ (Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire) and ROSA (Rapid Office Strain Assessment) methods. ). The results of research using the CMDQ method show that employees complain about the neck, shoulders, arms, back, waist, hips, buttocks, and need immediate improvement. The results of the ROSA calculation show that employee A, employee B, and employee C have a high or dangerous risk, and urgent improvements need to be made. The cause of the high risk experienced is due to the inadequate facilities used, the need to update work facilities according to ergonomic standards in the world of work, and holding good and correct computer office ergonomics training to reduce injuries when using computers.

documents.abstract: We propose a novel framework that re-architects explainable artificial intelligence within decision support systems by integrating persistent homology into the explanation pipeline. Conventional approaches treat local feature attributions, such as SHAP values, as isolated scalar values for individual predictions, thereby overlooking the multi-scale interaction structures that emerge across a dataset. To address this limitation, we embed a collection of local explanation vectors into a metric space and compute persistent homology using the Vietoris-Rips complex. This topological analysis yields a set of persistence diagrams that capture the birth and death of homology generators across multiple scales. From these diagrams, we construct a global interaction tensor that encodes the total persistence of topological features involving pairs of input features. This tensor is then incorporated into the decision support system’s utility model as a regularization term, which penalizes or rewards the co-occurrence of high-magnitude attributions on features that persistently interact across the dataset. The resulting system provides decision-makers with queryable, multi-scale explanations at selectable persistence thresholds, transforming the interface from a static explainer into a dynamic topological reasoning tool. For instance, a user can request all feature pairs with persistence above a given threshold in a specific homology dimension, and the system highlights those interactions in the explanation. The proposed method is realized using the Ripser algorithm for efficient computation on datasets of up to one hundred thousand instances, with periodic updates via a streaming variant. Our contribution is a principled mathematical framework that bridges topological data analysis and explainable AI, offering a new perspective on feature interaction discovery and explanation stability. The significance lies in its ability to reveal robust, higher-order interaction structures that are invisible to standard attribution methods, thereby enhancing the interpretability and trustworthiness of model-driven decisions.
topics: Homotopy and Cohomology in Algebraic Topology

documents.abstract: Guided wave (GW)-based damage localization in carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites is fundamentally challenged by thermal variations and sparse sensor configurations, which induce severe baseline distortions and imaging artifacts. Traditional physical algorithms suffer from geometric ambiguity, while purely data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) models are hindered by opaque interpretability and prohibitive data dependency. This paper proposes a physics-informed deep learning (PIDL) framework, an artificial-intelligence-driven approach, for few-shot damage localization under thermal variations. The network is architected with a dual-stream input design, comprising a data-driven layer enhanced by a one-dimensional coordinate attention (1D-CA) mechanism and a physics-informed layer built upon a differentiable time-of-flight (TOF) physical imaging layer. A hybrid physics-constrained loss function is formulated to suppress non-physical artifacts and enforce physical consistency. GW signals are experimentally collected from manufactured CFRP composite plates, and a comparative investigation is performed to thoroughly assess the PIDL performance. Results indicate that:(1) The presence of physical penalties effectively mitigates artifacts and achieves robust localization across thermal gradients; (2) The model demonstrates superior spatial generalization that the integration of acoustic physical constraints acts as a crucial regularization mechanism, maintaining a highly accurate mean relative error (MRE) of 3.88% on completely unseen damage coordinates; (3) By implementing a few-shot transfer learning strategy, the PIDL model shows adaptability for dynamic operational environments (45 degrees Celsius (°C)-75 degrees Celsius (°C)). This work offers a physically interpretable and data-efficient paradigm for structural health monitoring (SHM) in dynamic operational environments.

OBJECTIVES: Real-world implementation of large language models such as ChatGPT to enhance patient education remains limited. We evaluated the feasibility, acceptability and attitudes towards a ChatGPT-based counselling tool among patients and healthcare workers (HCWs) in a specialist infectious diseases clinic. METHODS: We conducted a prospective clinical implementation study in a specialist HIV and sexual health clinic in Singapore from Jan 2025 to December 2025. Patients interacted with a custom ChatGPT-based chatbot prior to routine counselling by physicians or pharmacists. Responses were reviewed with patients subsequently during consultation. Post-interaction, patients and HCWs completed structured surveys incorporating domains from a validated survey tool: perceived risk, anxiety, technology/social influence and intention for future use. RESULTS: The chatbot was most frequently used for counselling on antiretroviral therapy initiation or switching, and sexual health advice. A total of 35 patients and 35 HCW assessments were analysed. Patients had greater perceived risk with the use of the chatbot compared to HCWs, as indicated by lower median scores (13, IQR 10-16; vs. 18, IQR 15-21), while anxiety scores were similar. Technology/social influence scores were high across both groups (overall median 20, IQR 19-22). Most participants indicated willingness for future use. Qualitative feedback highlighted improved patient understanding and more focused consultations, but concerns included lack of contextual nuance and occasional inaccuracies. CONCLUSIONS: The pilot implementation of a ChatGPT-based counselling tool in a specialist HIV and sexual health clinic was feasible and generally acceptable to patients and HCWs. Further studies are required to evaluate accuracy and clinical effectiveness before broader implementation.

documents.abstract: Introduction: Ischemic heart disease represents one of the most prevalent conditions characterized by elevated mortality rates. The aim of this research was to provide an efficient instrument for the early diagnosis of ischemic heart disease and to assist clinical decision-making processes through the application of hybrid artificial intelligence algorithms. Methods: The data used in this study were from Yazd Health Study (YaHS) enrollment phase dataset, comprising 9969 participants and 30 selective features from a total of 300, collected between 2014 to 2015. Data were analyzed using SVM and XGBoost machine learning algorithms using Python version 3.11.8. Results: Combining the strengths of SVM and XGBoost models through a Voting Classifier approach enhanced both the accuracy and efficiency of the heart disease prediction model. When evaluating the predictive performance for heart disease, the Voting Classifier model achieved in accuracy rate of 90%. Conclusion: These findings suggest that implementing machine learning techniques and hybrid algorithms for early diagnosis and prediction could facilitate earlier intervention in CHD, ultimately helping to lower mortality rates.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) shifts educational focus from access to information toward judging machine-generated claims and regulating the division of epistemic work. This conceptual article proposes the SAM model—self-regulation (S), ambiguity tolerance (A), and methodological competence (M)—as a bounded person-level resource model within broader AI readiness, with educators’ AI readiness as a central application. S denotes regulatory capacity, A a disposition-like willingness to tolerate unresolved epistemic ambiguity, and M the capacity to evaluate claims, differentiated into cross-domain M1 and domain-specific M2. SAM’s distinctive claim is configurational: M should predict independently assessed judgment more strongly at higher S and, under high ambiguity, when A is higher. These relations, the M1/M2 distinction, limited compensability, and incremental prediction beyond shared and neighboring accounts remain hypothetical. The model separates resources from enacted processes, contextual affordances, and outcomes and requires independent performance criteria. For AI-based assessment and learning analytics, educators’ interpretations of AI-derived evidence and construct inferences from behavioral traces require validated mappings addressing alternative explanations, comparability, fairness, and use. SAM thus offers a research agenda predicting when AI support preserves human judgment rather than merely improving supported performance.

Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. Implications for practice and/or policy Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI systems. Developers and educators aiming to design pedagogically meaningful GenAI tools should focus on scaffolding SRL both cognitively and emotionally, to support the affective and self‐regulatory dimensions of learning. We make the technical specifications and system prompts publicly available.

documents.abstract: Background. Dependence on generative and conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is measured with diverse instruments spanning addiction criteria, task reliance, and emotional bonding. No meta-analysis has pooled its psychological correlates across populations. Methods. We conducted a pre-registered three-level meta-analysis (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.23420672) searching eight electronic databases and citations of instrument papers on 16 October 2026, with citation chasing. Zero-order correlations were pooled using correlated and hierarchical effects models on Fisher's z with cluster-robust inference (CR2). Scale type (T1 addiction-type, T2 functional, T3 emotional, T4 mixed) was the primary moderator. Certainty was rated via GRADE. Results. We included 127 samples (123 studies; N = 74,492; 29 countries; 70% university students; 39% mainland China). AI dependence correlated moderately with anxiety (r = 0.37, 95% CI [0.25, 0.48]), stress (r = 0.35 [0.25, 0.43]), depression (r = 0.32 [0.21, 0.42]), social anxiety (r = 0.36 [0.17, 0.53]), loneliness (r = 0.28 [0.18, 0.38]), and procrastination (r = 0.26 [0.12, 0.40]), and weakly and inversely with self-esteem (r = −0.18 [−0.35, −0.00]). All 95% prediction intervals crossed zero. Addiction-type and mixed scales showed no detectable difference; functional and emotional scales were rarely paired with clinical outcomes. Certainty was low to very low. Conclusions. AI dependence moderately correlates with distress and self-regulation difficulties, but prediction intervals cross zero and evidence certainty is low. Functional and emotional dependence have rarely been studied alongside clinical outcomes.

The rapid growth of influencer marketing has created diverse opportunities for the brands to interact with the consumers. At the same time, concerns regarding manipulated follower counts, artificial engagement and questionable influencer authenticity have become increasingly relevant. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is used as a technological mechanism for finding skeptical patterns and supporting fraud detection. However, the use and acceptance of these systems are largely influenced by consumers’ perceptions and trust. The present study focuses trust and concerns of consumers regarding AI-driven fraud detection and consumer attitudes towards transparency, AI-based verification and measures intended to strengthen authenticity in influencer marketing. The study adopts a descriptive research design and uses primary data collected from 70 respondents through a structured questionnaire. The findings show that respondents demonstrate cautious acceptance of AI-driven fraud detection. Half of the respondents reported that they somewhat trust AI, whereas complete trust was comparatively limited. Concerns relating to transparency, privacy, false identification and possible bias were also identified. The findings further reveal that consumers attach considerable importance to transparency and generally support AI-based verification systems. Respondents also expressed favourable opinions regarding the use of AI tools by brands while evaluating influencers for collaboration. The study concludes that AI can contribute to improving authenticity in influencer marketing, but its acceptance depends on the development of transparent, reliable and accountable systems.

documents.abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped drug discovery. AI-based models typically rely on molecular representations for prediction. However, the absence of physically grounded information in mainstream molecular representations not only limits the model performance in practical applications but also hinders mechanistic understanding and exploitation by humans. To overcome this issue, we introduce qcGEM, a quantum-chemistry-aware graph-based embedding of molecules that incorporates physical priors into molecular representation learning. Through a specially designed model architecture to adequately process quantum chemistry information, qcGEM provides a compact, physics-informed molecular representation that supports a diverse range of downstream applications. Particularly, qcGEM demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of molecule-related benchmarks, as evidenced by comprehensive evaluations on 83 tasks including molecular property prediction, activity cliff detection, protein-ligand interaction modeling, and opioid drug regression, and simultaneously offers strong interpretability at multiple representation levels. We additionally propose a simplified variant, qcGEM-Hybrid, with substantially accelerated embedding generation and robust performance. Overall, our method provides an advanced molecular representation that will benefit molecule-related modeling and prediction, supporting further progress in AI-aided drug discovery.

documents.abstract: There is a deep structural crisis at the intersection of clinical medicine and criminal law in England and Wales. This paper attacks the use of the common law principle of gross negligence manslaughter (GNM) in response to involuntary clinical error and argues that the existing legal framework is driven by an unprincipled regimen of single agency fault. This approach compresses complicated, multi-factorial institutional failures into the sole criminal liability of the practitioner on duty, equating an unfortunate consequence with the blameworthy. Using a dual-axis framework that integrates doctrinal legal analysis with socio-technical systems theory and human factors engineering, this paper analyzes the institutional processes leading to and shaping key judicial decisions and considers the actual nature of health care. This study concludes that current legal approaches do not advance patient safety, and, post- pandemic, contribute to an unacknowledged, destructive diffuse risk for health professionals, ultimately inducing systematic defensive medicine, which in turn creates new safety hazards and fundamentally undermines patient- practitioner interaction. While the principle of a "just culture" has been called for in the context of administrative review, this aspirational goal is systemically undermining by the retributive rules of the criminal justice system. This paper concludes with concrete legal reform suggestions; to both codify a statutory framework and to adopt a subjective recklessness standard, ensuring criminal law responds only to criminal intent and to systemic institutional factors that the system's penal framework fails to address.

AIM: To describe registered nurses' experiences of clinical decision-making and identify needs that may inform future development of artificial-intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. DESIGN: A qualitative descriptive study. METHODS: Data were collected between 2022 and 2025 through 16 semi-structured interviews with registered nurses working in inpatient wards at a Finnish university hospital. The data were analysed using inductive content analysis. RESULTS: Perceived challenges in clinical decision-making were related to organisational issues, multiprofessional collaboration, nurse-patient interactions, professional factors and availability and trustworthiness of data. The findings also identified support needs related to health information management, clinical workflows and quality of nursing care that may inform future artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support system development. CONCLUSION: Nurses experienced multifaceted challenges and needs in clinical decision-making, shaped by organisational, professional, relational and information-related factors. Adoption of artificial intelligence-assisted decision support systems may represent one potential approach to optimising clinical decision-making, improving patient care quality and enhancing workflow efficiency. Realising these opportunities requires coordinated efforts at individual, organisational and societal levels, including competence development, workflow redesign, strong data governance and a culture that fosters trust in technology. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: The findings may inform the future development of artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. REPORTING METHOD: The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research checklist was used when reporting the results. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: Registered nurses participated in the study. IMPACT: What problem did the study address? This paper addresses existing gaps and unmet needs in nursing clinical decision-making What were the main findings? The main findings highlight several key opportunities for artificial intelligence-assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The research may inform efforts to optimise health information management, streamline clinical workflows and improve the quality of nursing care.

documents.abstract: Psychological resilience in elite sport concerns adaptation to sustained and acute demands, not the simple absence of distress. This critical integrative review examines how religious meaning-making and religious coping might interact with mental toughness, challenge appraisal, social resources, and human performance under high-performance conditions. It distinguishes resilience as a dynamic process from mental toughness as a contested psychological construct and separates athlete well-being from competitive outcomes. Evidence is synthesized from sport-specific resilience research, religion-and-sport scholarship, established religious-coping measures, and elite-athlete mental-health literature. A conditional, multidimensional framework is proposed in which personally endorsed beliefs may influence the interpretation of stressors, access to support, and persistence, while spiritual struggle, external religious pressure, or rigid ritual dependence may undermine adaptation. The available literature supports examining these pathways but does not establish that religious affiliation directly improves performance or confers immunity from psychological difficulties. The article develops falsifiable propositions and a research design involving longitudinal measurements, contextual stress exposure, validated comparator measures, objective performance indices, and athlete-led qualitative accounts. Its practical recommendations prioritize autonomy, culturally responsive support, clinical referral where indicated, and avoidance of coercive spiritual practices. No new participants or original experimental data are reported. The proposed framework is a hypothesis for empirical testing rather than a validated screening tool or causal finding. elite athletes; psychological resilience; mental toughness; religious coping; stress appraisal; human performance

Investment behaviour has changed as a result of artificial intelligence (AI), which replaces human judgment with data-driven insights. Investors may analyse big information, spot trends, and optimize portfolios with the help of technologies like machine learning, robo-advisors, and predictive analytics, increasing productivity and lowering emotional biases. Adoption of AI is not without its difficulties, though, such as algorithmic bias, a lack of transparency, expensive costs, and problems with data quality. Automation bias and market volatility may increase if automated systems are overused. This study highlights AI’s impact on investor behaviour and emphasizes the importance of a balanced, responsible approach to effectively integrate AI into investment decision-making processes.

Role of Artificial Intelligence in Modern Banking Services: Benefits, Customer Experience and Challenges This research investigates the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in modern banking services, with particular emphasis on operational efficiency, customer experience, and emerging challenges. It examines the application of AI-driven technologies, including machine learning, intelligent chatbots, predictive analytics, and automated fraud detection, in streamlining banking operations, enhancing service personalisation, improving risk management, and supporting data-driven decision-making. Furthermore, the study evaluates key concerns associated with AI adoption, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, transparency, and customer trust. By assessing both the benefits and limitations of AI integration, this research aims to develop a comprehensive understanding of its implications for the banking sector and highlight the importance of responsible, secure, and customer-centric AI implementation in the evolving financial services landscape.

An AI agent can be given an objective by a human, then search, interpret, plan, use tools, and act before returning a result. The human remains present. But how much of this activity can they still understand, verify, or influence? Savoir / Action begins with this difficulty. The manuscript examines the relationship between the knowledge an AI agent treats as valid, the means it uses to act, and the constraints that shape its trajectory. It asks what human supervision can still mean when control cannot be reduced to permissions, a stop button, or approval of the final result. This reflection grew out of exploratory work conducted within a human–AI dyad. We have chosen to make this origin explicit because it is part of the very question we are examining. We do not claim to have established a theory. We present our thinking as it stands: some distinctions have become clearer, some questions remain open, and several propositions still need to be challenged by other perspectives. This is the canonical English translation of the original French manuscript, first published on 5 October 2026: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23164286
